hook_clip: Here's how to reverse engineer Statuspage from a written spec. Claude passed all eighteen checks, and found fifty-eight gaps in my spec.
outro_clip: The full spec is free at personal software factory dot com. If you build it, tell me what broke. I'm Sam. See you tomorrow.

scenes.text: We gave Claude one Markdown file. It copies the part of Atlassian Statuspage a small software team needs. Each part of the product gets a live status. Incidents get timed updates. Maintenance starts and ends on time. And customers subscribe by email to only the parts they use.

The core rule is uptime. Every status change is written to a log that's never edited. Uptime over ninety days counts every minute of major outage, and half of every minute of partial outage. Degraded and maintenance count as up. So forty-two minutes of API outage shows as ninety-nine point nine six percent, rounded down.

Claude built it in four phases, one prompt each. The foundation and the public page. Incidents and maintenance. Subscribers, emails, the feed and the API. Then automation and postmortems. After every phase, the acceptance checks ran in a real browser, from fresh seed data.

Here's what it built. The public page shows each component with ninety daily bars, and one red day for the API. The incident page lists every update, newest first. Owen starts a new incident from a template, with a preview of the subscriber email. His dashboard now shows a partial outage. And the outbox holds the email, with its one-click unsubscribe link.
In one final run, on a fresh database, all eighteen checks passed, along with one hundred and fourteen automated tests.

But the more useful result is what broke. The test build exposed fifty-eight places where Claude had to guess. A hidden component could still set the banner for the whole page. Caching a subscriber's own page could show their email address to the next visitor. And one check said C D T, which was wrong once daylight saving ended. Every gap is now fixed in the spec.

Passing every check isn't the same as production-ready. We didn't test production sign-in, real email delivery, the every-minute job on a real scheduler, a real monitoring tool, or hosting it apart from your product. Those are yours to check before customers rely on it.

So is it worth building? Statuspage is free for one hundred subscribers and two team members. Paid plans run from twenty-nine to fourteen hundred and ninety-nine dollars a month, and subscribing to single components starts on Business, at three hundred and ninety-nine. If you need text messages, Slack alerts or private pages, buy it. If you want component subscriptions on your own domain, build it.
Everything is in one file. The data model, twelve rules, seed data, four phase prompts, and all eighteen checks, with the fifty-eight fixes already in.
